analysis.one_liner: Bans credit default swaps outright and hands the SEC authority over all security-based swaps.
analysis.headline: A bill to make credit default swaps illegal was introduced during the financial crisis but never received a hearing or vote, dying in committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for anyone to enter into a credit default swap — a side bet on whether a company or loan will default — and would have given the Securities and Exchange Commission power to register and police other security-based swaps. The bill's stated reasoning was that uncollateralized speculation in these contracts spread through the financial system and destroyed wealth during the 2008 crisis. Instead of a ban, the eventual 2010 law (Dodd-Frank) kept the swaps legal but pushed them toward exchanges and clearinghouses.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and savers, who bore the cost of the 2008 bailouts when unregulated swap positions threatened major institutions. The bill would have removed the tool that let financial firms pile up hidden, uncollateralized bets against loans and bonds, reducing the chance that taxpayers again get billed to rescue institutions whose losses came from these contracts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and savers exposed to bailout risk

how_it_helps.text: Declares it unlawful for any person to enter into a credit default swap agreement or contract, taking effect 180 days after enactment [S3].
Gives the SEC authority over all security-based swap agreements, including power to require registration and to issue rules against fraud, manipulation, and insider trading in swaps [S2].

Cites as findings that parties wrote credit default swaps without posting collateral, creating systemic risk, and that the contracts 'caused significant wealth destruction during our economic crisis' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, broker-dealers, and hedge funds that earn fees from writing and trading credit default swaps, and large institutions that use them to hedge their own bond and loan exposure — they would lose the market entirely rather than operate under new rules. Businesses that borrow could also face somewhat costlier credit if lenders lose a tool for hedging their loans.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a flat ban rather than regulation. Credit default swaps also serve a legitimate purpose — a lender or bondholder can buy protection against a borrower defaulting — so an outright prohibition removes that hedging tool and could make some credit more expensive [S3].
The ban takes effect 180 days after enactment, so existing contracts entered into before that date remain in force; the transition away from an existing market could be abrupt [S3].

A total ban was far more sweeping than what Congress ultimately enacted; the Dodd-Frank Act instead kept swaps legal with exchange trading, clearing, and reporting requirements, a route that preserves hedging uses while addressing the hidden-risk problem [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real problem — a large, opaque, uncollateralized market that amplified the 2008 crisis — but it addressed it with the bluntest possible tool. Banning the entire market, including hedging by lenders and bondholders who genuinely own the underlying debt, goes beyond what most financial reformers proposed; the law that eventually passed chose strict regulation over prohibition. The bill's main value was as an early marker of how far reform could go; its design was not what became policy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Maxine Waters introduced the bill on July 9, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1].
The complete action history contains only those two entries — introduction and committee referral — with no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action [S5].
Congress chose a different path: the financial reform law enacted in 2010 regulated swaps under exchange trading, clearing, and reporting rules rather than banning them [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other institutions that write and trade credit default swaps are better off — the market they profit from was never closed, and the subsequent reform law regulated it rather than eliminating it. The swap market has continued largely intact since.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban credit default swaps and give the SEC swap oversight.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled on the bill.

against.name: Wall Street swap dealers and hedge funds
against.what_they_did: Opposed bans and strict mandates on over-the-counter derivatives during the 2009-2010 financial reform debate, pushing for regulation short of prohibition.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split is recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Banks and broker-dealers that write and trade credit default swaps
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated their credit default swap business outright, a market worth trillions in notional value at the time. Its interest ran against the public's in this bill: the swaps' uncollateralized growth created the systemic risk that taxpayers absorbed in the 2008 bailouts, and the industry's continued access to the market was preserved when the bill died.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and other speculative traders
industries.note: The bill specifically targeted speculation by parties with no stake in the underlying loan or bond — 'naked' credit default swaps [S3]. Killing the market ends that speculation entirely.

industries.industry: Bond and loan investors who hedge with swaps
industries.note: These buyers use credit default swaps for legitimate protection against defaults, and a total ban removes that tool; the bill's sponsors argued the same market's speculative side caused broader harm. Their gains and losses genuinely cut both ways here.
